Interactions

The composite controls, each one a field or a button plus an overlay and a keyboard contract. The popover is the primitive the rest are built on: get its placement, dismissal and focus behavior right once and the combobox and the pickers inherit all three.

Popovers

Anchored content that can be interacted with. A .tooltip only describes and cannot be reached by the keyboard; a .menu is a list of actions and closes on any of them. A popover is neither: it holds fields, summaries, pickers — anything — and stays open until it is dismissed.

A popover is not modal. The page behind it stays live, so it can explain a field without taking the field away.

filter_list Filter results
AL

Ada Lovelace

Analytical engines

View profile

data-placement states a preference. It is swapped automatically when the chosen side has no room — try this near the right edge.

Escape dismisses and returns focus to the trigger. A click outside dismisses without moving focus, because the pointer has already decided where to go.

Markup

<div class="popover-anchor">
  <button class="button button-outlined" type="button" data-popover="pop-id">Filter</button>

  <div class="popover" id="pop-id" data-placement="bottom" aria-label="Filter">
    <!-- anything -->
    <button class="button button-text" type="button" data-popover-close>Done</button>
  </div>
</div>

Command palette

One modal search over everything the page can do. Structurally it is the combobox below, moved into a dialog: the input never loses focus, and the arrow keys move a selection it points at with aria-activedescendant.

Press Ctrl + K anywhere on this page.

The trigger matters as much as the shortcut. A palette reachable only by a key combination is reachable only by people who have been told it exists, which is why this one sits in the page as a visible control with its shortcut printed on it.

It is an accelerator and never the only route to a command. Every entry below is something the page can also do some other way — if an action lives only here, it is missing from the interface.

Markup

<div class="palette-scrim" id="app-palette" data-palette data-open="false">
  <div class="palette" role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-label="Commands">
    <div class="palette-search">
      <span class="icon">search</span>
      <input class="palette-input" type="text" placeholder="Type a command…">
    </div>
    <ul class="palette-list">
      <li class="palette-group-label" data-group="Go to">Go to</li>
      <li class="palette-item" data-group="Go to"
          data-keywords="color type scale" data-href="foundations.html">
        <span class="icon">palette</span>
        <span class="palette-item-text">
          <span class="palette-item-title">Foundations</span>
        </span>
      </li>
    </ul>
    <p class="palette-empty" hidden>No matching command.</p>
  </div>
</div>

An item with data-href navigates. Any other item fires a ui:command event carrying its data-command, so a page decides what each one does without this kit knowing any of them. data-keywords is matched alongside the label, which is how "color" finds Foundations.

Comboboxes

A text field that filters a listbox. The field keeps real focus the whole time and the highlighted row is published through aria-activedescendant, which is what lets the arrow keys move a screen reader's attention without focus ever leaving the input. Use this instead of a <select> once the list is long enough that scanning it is slower than typing.

Date pickers

<input type="date"> is one of the controls whose appearance no token can reach — every browser draws its own calendar. This replaces it: a text field for typing, a popover calendar for picking, and a hidden field carrying the ISO value either way.

The markup below is the long form, and it is what you write when the field needs something the short form cannot express. The short form is data-picker on a plain <input type="date">, which the script expands into exactly this; data-picker="native" keeps the browser’s. The input types section on the forms page is where that choice is set out, and it covers all six upgradeable types at once.

The field shows a readable date; the form submits YYYY-MM-DD.

Bounded by data-min and data-max; days outside are unselectable.

Always visible

The same calendar without a popover around it, for a booking screen where picking a date is the whole point of the page.

Why local time, not UTC

A date chosen from a calendar is a calendar date, not an instant. Parsing 2026-10-20 with new Date(string) treats it as midnight UTC, which is the 19th for anyone west of Greenwich. Every date in this kit is built from its year, month and day parts in local time, so the day that was clicked is the day that is stored. 

/* Wrong: shifts by a day depending on where you are. */
new Date('2026-10-20');

/* Right: the parts mean what they say, wherever you are. */
new Date(2026, 9, 20);

Keyboard, inside the grid

KeyMoves
← →One day
↑ ↓One week
Home / EndStart / end of the week
PgUp / PgDnOne month, carrying the day across
EnterChooses the focused day and closes

The grid is one tab stop, not forty-two. Arrow keys move a roving tabindex between the days, which is the pattern every grid in this kit uses.

Time pickers

Scrolling columns rather than a clock face: faster to hit with a pointer, and the only form that works at a phone's width without a modal. The stored value is always twenty-four-hour HH:MM whatever the field displays.

Quarter-hour steps, twelve-hour display.

data-hour-cycle="24" drops the meridiem column — right for anything an operator reads.

Typing is always allowed: 9:30, 09:30 and 9:30 pm are all understood, and anything else leaves the previous value alone.

Date and time

One field, one value, two panels side by side. It owns neither panel: the markup holds a real date picker and a real time picker, each with its own hidden value, and the data-datetimepicker behavior does nothing but join the pair into YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM when either half commits. A second calendar renderer would be a second calendar to fix.

Below 560 pixels the two panels stack rather than squeeze.

Month pickers

A year with twelve cells in it, not a calendar with the days switched off. A month is neither a date nor a range — billing periods, report windows and expiry dates are months, and treating one as “the first of” is how an off-by-one lands in an invoice.

Stores YYYY-MM; shows the month by name.

min and max carry over; months outside are unselectable.

Color pickers

<input type="color"> opens the operating system’s color dialog — the one surface in a page that no stylesheet has ever been able to touch. A Windows color dialog opening out of a dark page is not a quieter version of this kit, it is a different program, so the kit draws its own.

Three sliders and a hex box, not a two-dimensional gradient field with a draggable dot. The dot is the better mouse control and the worse everything else: it has no keyboard story that is not invented, it needs a pointer-move loop to be any good, and it cannot say what it currently is without a readout beside it anyway. Hue, saturation and lightness as three range inputs are arrow-key operable for free, announce their own values, and are the slider this kit already has. Each track is drawn along its own axis at the current hue, so it previews what moving it would do rather than being a neutral rail.

The swatch row is the part most people will use, and it is the kit’s own token colors read off the live custom properties — so it follows the theme, follows a retheme, and makes the common case of picking a color that belongs to this design language one click that cannot go wrong. data-presets on the wrapper replaces the row with a list of your own.

The hex is the field, so it can be typed, pasted and copied.

The tick on a swatch is drawn in whichever of black or white reads on it.

Tag fields

Several values in one box, each a chip. Reach for this when the set is open-ended — labels, recipients, keywords. When the values come from a fixed list, a multiple combobox is the better control, because it stops a typo becoming a new tag.

CSS Accessibility

Enter or a comma adds one. Backspace twice removes the last.

Pasting a comma-separated list adds every address in it, which is how addresses actually arrive.

The first Backspace on an empty field arms the last chip rather than deleting it; the second removes it. One keystroke should not silently destroy a value.

Number steppers

A themed replacement for the native spin buttons, which are around 10 pixels tall and unstyleable. The buttons are out of the tab order on purpose: the field is the control, and the arrow keys step it — along with Page Up and Page Down for ten at a time, and Home and End for the bounds.

Those keys are the kit’s, not the browser’s, because the field is no longer type="number" once the script has it. It ships as one, so that it still steps and still gets a numeric keypad with the script turned off, and is downgraded to text on upgrade. That is not cosmetic: a number field refuses setSelectionRange, and Firefox selects the whole value whenever focus arrives from script rather than from a click — so pressing a step button left the field flooded with selection highlight that only a click elsewhere would clear. A text field lets the caret be put back where it belongs. role="spinbutton" and the value attributes carry to assistive technology what the type no longer does.

0 to 10. The buttons disable at the bounds.

Decimal places come from the step, so 4.50 never shows as 4.5000000001.

For a table cell or a toolbar.

Ratings

An interactive rating is a radio group wearing stars, which is why the arrow keys work and a form submits it without help. A reported average is not a control at all, so it is drawn as plain output with the number beside it — a shape alone is not a readable figure.

Interactive

data-rating-labels gives each value a word, so the readout says "Very good" rather than "4 of 5".

Reported

starstarstarstarstar starstarstarstarstar 4.3 · 1,284 reviews
starstarstarstarstar starstarstarstarstar 2.5 · 31 reviews

A fraction is drawn by clipping a filled row over an empty one, so 4.3 looks like 4.3 rather than rounding to 4. The row carries role="img" and one label, because five separate star icons announce as noise.

One-time codes

Several boxes that behave like one field. The split is worth it because it shows the expected length before anything is typed, which is most of what makes a code entry feel quick.

Six digits

–

Paste the whole code into any box and it spreads across the rest. Backspace on an empty box steps back and clears the one before it.

Rejected

error That code has expired. Request a new one.

The first box carries autocomplete="one-time-code", which is what lets a phone offer the code straight from the message.

Split buttons

One obvious action plus its variations. Use it when there is a clear default that most people want and a handful who need something adjacent — "Save" beside "Save as a copy". When no option is the obvious default, use a plain menu button instead.

The toggle half needs its own label. Without one it announces as "button" and there is no way to know it opens anything.

Speed dials

A floating action button that fans out. It earns its place when a screen has three or four ways to create something and no room for three or four buttons; past about five it becomes a menu that happens to float.

A screen's worth of content, with the dial over it.

Document
Image
Folder

Collapsed actions leave the tab order as well as the screen. A button nobody can see but Tab still reaches is worse than no button at all.

Inline editing

Text that becomes a field in the same place, at the same size, so nothing moves when it is clicked. Right for a correction — a title, a label, one cell. Wrong for anything that needs validating against other fields, which belongs in a form.

A heading

In a table

Without explicit buttons, Enter commits and Escape reverts. Clicking away commits too, which is what people expect; Escape is the way back out.

Reordering

Dragging is the obvious way and the only one some people cannot use, so the handle is also a button: Enter picks the row up, the arrow keys move it, Enter drops it. Every move is announced, because otherwise the whole interaction is invisible without sight of the list.

The row you grab is the row that moves: it lifts out of the list, follows the pointer, and leaves a dashed gap where it came from so you can still see what you are undoing. The drop line stays — it marks a position between two rows, which the floating row cannot.

  • Triage incoming reports
  • Review open pull requests
  • Update the deployment runbook
  • Rotate the signing keys
  • Archive last quarter's boards

Pointer events rather than HTML5 drag-and-drop, which does nothing at all on a touch screen. touch-action: none on the handle is what stops a drag turning into a page scroll.

A list taller than its box

Where carrying the row earns its keep. Drag one to the top or bottom edge and the list scrolls itself, faster the closer you get, and stops when it runs out — so a row can reach a position that was never on screen when you picked it up. The drop line keeps up while the list moves under a pointer that is standing still, which is the part that is easy to get wrong. The arrow keys do the same thing without the pointer: the list follows the row rather than the row vanishing off the edge.

  • Rotate the staging credentials
  • Split the migration into two releases
  • Retire the v1 webhook endpoint
  • Backfill the missing audit rows
  • Document the rate limit headers
  • Cache the pricing page at the edge
  • Replace the polling status widget
  • Alert on the queue depth, not the queue age
  • Move the nightly export off the primary
  • Write the on-call handover template
  • Delete the three unused feature flags
  • Pin the build image to a digest

The same mechanism carries the cards on the board, which needs it more: a card there crosses columns, so it has two scrollers to outrun rather than one. It is one piece of code, not two that drifted apart.

Turning it off

data-drag-proxy="off" on the list — or on anything above it, up to <body>, since the nearest one wins — drops back to drop lines and a faded row, which is honest but harder to follow. A nested list can turn it back on with "on". It is on by default because the cost of the other default is paid by whoever is dragging, not by whoever chose it.

UI.lift() is the same mechanism on its own, for a drag the kit does not already cover: hand it the element and the pointer position, call move() on each pointer move and drop() once the element is where it belongs, and it takes care of the carry, the gap, the scrolling and the landing. UI.lift.edge, .speed and .settle are the three numbers worth changing.

Choosing a control

Several of these overlap. The deciding question is usually how many options there are, and whether they are known in advance.

SituationControlWhy not the others
Two to five known options Radio buttons or a segmented control All of them visible at once beats any control that hides them behind a click.
Six to about fifteen known options A combobox with data-filter="none" Short enough to scan, so typeahead is overhead. A native select would work, but its list cannot be themed.
More options than fit on a screen A filtering combobox Scrolling a hundred rows is slower than typing three letters.
Several values from a known set A combobox with data-multiple A tag field would let a typo become a new value.
Several values, open-ended A tag field There is no list to pick from, so there is nothing to filter.
A number in a narrow range A number stepper A slider is for approximate values; it cannot express "exactly 7".
A number whose exact value does not matter A slider A stepper invites precision the value does not have.
A date near today A date picker Typing is faster for a distant date, which is why the field stays typeable.
A date of birth A plain text field, or three selects Nobody wants to page back eighty years through a calendar.
Extra detail about something on screen A popover A dialog takes the page away to say one sentence.
